A TCP connection begins with a process called the three-way handshake, which establishes a reliable communication channel between a client and server. The client initiates the process by sending a SYN (synchronization) packet to the server, which includes an initial sequence number that helps both sides track the order of data being transmitted. The server receives this SYN packet and responds with a SYN-ACK packet, which acknowledges the client's sequence number and provides its own initial sequence number. The client then sends an ACK (acknowledgment) packet back to the server, confirming that it has received the server's sequence number. Once this three-way handshake completes successfully, the connection is established and both sides can begin exchanging data reliably. This handshake mechanism ensures that both the client and server are ready to communicate and that they can recognize and properly order the packets they exchange.

Once the connection is open, data flows between the client and server with TCP ensuring reliable delivery through a system of sequence numbers and acknowledgments. Each side maintains a send buffer containing data waiting to be transmitted and a receive buffer for incoming data. When one side sends data, it includes sequence numbers so the receiving side can reassemble packets in the correct order even if they arrive out of sequence. The receiving side sends acknowledgment packets back to the sender, confirming which data bytes have been successfully received and asking the sender to retransmit any missing packets. TCP also implements flow control using a mechanism called the sliding window, which allows the receiver to tell the sender how much data it can accept at any given time, preventing the sender from overwhelming the receiver with too much data at once. This back-and-forth exchange of data and acknowledgments continues for as long as the application needs to communicate.

Keeping a TCP connection alive over long periods requires mechanisms to detect when a connection has become inactive or when the other side has unexpectedly disconnected. Applications can use TCP keep-alive probes, which send small packets periodically when no data has been exchanged for a while, allowing both sides to confirm that the connection is still active and working. If the application sends data regularly, these keep-alive probes are unnecessary because the acknowledgments on the data packets already serve to confirm the connection is healthy. Firewalls and network devices may also close idle connections after a certain amount of time, so applications that need persistent connections often send periodic heartbeat messages as part of their application protocol. Timeouts are configured at the operating system level or application level to detect when the remote side has become unresponsive, allowing the local side to abandon the connection after a certain period of inactivity. Some applications use TCP's built-in keep-alive option, which can be enabled on a socket to have the operating system automatically send probe packets if the connection remains idle.

The closure of a TCP connection is a carefully orchestrated process to ensure that both sides agree the connection is ending and that all data in transit has been successfully delivered before the connection is fully torn down. The side that wants to close the connection first sends a FIN (finish) packet, signaling to the other side that it has finished sending data and will not send any more. The receiving side acknowledges this FIN packet with an ACK and may continue to send data if it has pending information to transmit, though it knows no more data will arrive from the initiating side. Once the receiving side has finished sending its own data, it sends its own FIN packet to the initiating side. The initiating side then acknowledges this second FIN packet with an ACK, and at this point both sides agree the connection is closed. This four-way exchange, known as the four-way handshake or FIN handshake, ensures that both sides have finished communicating and have had an opportunity to complete any pending operations before the connection is fully released.

In some cases, an application or network condition may cause an abrupt connection termination that bypasses the graceful four-way handshake. When an application crashes or closes its socket without sending a proper FIN packet, or when a network error makes communication impossible, the connection is reset using a packet with the RST (reset) flag set. This RST packet tells the other side that the connection is being forcefully terminated and should not be used, and it does not wait for acknowledgment from the remote side. Both sides immediately discard any pending data and close their end of the connection without the normal handshake process. While abrupt resets are sometimes unavoidable, they carry a risk that some data in flight may be lost since there is no negotiation to ensure all data has been received. For this reason, applications that need reliability should always attempt to close connections gracefully using the FIN handshake whenever possible.

After a connection is fully closed, the operating system on both sides goes through a cleanup phase to release the resources that were allocated to that connection, such as memory buffers and file handles. The side that initiated the close enters a state called TIME_WAIT for a period of time (typically two to four minutes) during which it keeps track of closed connections and discards any stray packets that arrive late for that connection. This TIME_WAIT state is important because packets from the closed connection may still be traveling through the network or sitting in buffers, and discarding them prevents confusion with new connections that might use the same port numbers in the future. The other side closes its resources more quickly and returns to a state where it can accept new connections. The operating system on both sides eventually removes all internal tracking information for the connection, freeing up socket numbers and memory for new connections. Once this cleanup is complete, the connection is entirely gone and the resources it consumed are available for other applications or connections to use.
